discovery: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated many-body systems with ultracold atoms in optical lattices

nominees.name: Immanuel Bloch
nominees.affiliation: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics, Garching, and Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Germany

nominees.name: Peter Zoller
nominees.affiliation: University of Innsbruck and IQOQI, Austrian Academy of Sciences, Austria

nominees.name: J. Ignacio Cirac
nominees.affiliation: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics, Garching, Germany

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum many-body physics
motivation: In 1998 Zoller, Cirac and coworkers proposed that cold atoms in optical lattices realise the Bose-Hubbard model, with laser light setting the parameters. In 2002 Bloch and coworkers observed the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition, showing that an atomic gas can be made into a clean, controllable model of a strongly correlated solid. This was the start of analogue quantum simulation, as Feynman had imagined it. Over two decades the three of them, Cirac and Zoller in theory and Bloch in experiment, have built it into a mature field. Its tools include single-site quantum-gas microscopy, artificial gauge fields, many-body localisation and the study of quantum dynamics far from equilibrium. These are problems that classical computers cannot handle. Here atomic physics directly answers open questions in condensed-matter physics and quantum information, and it underpins today's programmable quantum simulators.
